title: Code Diffusion Models Are Continuous Human Noise Operators

contributions.purpose: Test whether the intermediate discrete representations produced during reverse code-diffusion resemble the mistakes humans actually make, i.e. whether code diffusion acts as a 'continuous human noise operator'.
contributions.mechanism: Analysis of pre-trained CodeFusion diffusion trajectories: measure, over diffusion time-steps, the number of tokens changed and the maximum distance between edited tokens (localization); compare diffusion-generated errors against human-error operators (BIFI, FLAME) and GPT-4o along localization, diversity, and complexity.
contributions.evaluation: Figure 2 shows fewer and more localized edits near the end of diffusion (global repairs first, then local); diffusion-generated data has higher diversity, higher complexity and more global errors than existing generators and GPT-4o.
contributions.source_quote: In this paper, we address those challenging by asking if code diffusion can serve as a continuous human noise operator? In other words, we evaluate the extent to which the discrete representations obtained during reverse diffusion steps ... are representative of mistakes that humans actually make.

contributions.purpose: Directly use a pre-trained code diffusion model for last-mile repair of broken code without training a specialized repair system.
contributions.mechanism: Inject a broken code snippet by adding noise to it and resuming the reverse diffusion process, letting the model denoise it back to compilable code; choose noise level via any%/best%/vote% strategies.
contributions.evaluation: Repairs 56.4-68.2% of Python and Excel snippets across noise levels; a small 60M-param diffusion model outperforms Codex on Python (+8%) and PowerShell (+11%); still underperforms dedicated systems (BIFI, LaMirage) and GPT-4o/RING with compiler feedback.
contributions.source_quote: First, we can leverage the diffusion model for last-mile repair by adding noise to a broken code snippet and resuming the diffusion process.

contributions.purpose: Overcome the long-tail training-data and out-of-distribution problems in training efficient last-mile repair systems by generating synthetic (broken, fixed) code pairs.
contributions.mechanism: Sample an intermediate program (input) and the final program (output) from the diffusion process to produce synthetic training pairs, then fine-tune cheaper repair models on them.
contributions.evaluation: Fine-tuning codet5-small, phi-3.5-mini and mistral-7b on diffusion-generated data gives +2.5-3.5% higher performance than existing generators and GPT-4o; authors state synthetic-data generation shows the most promise of the two applications.
contributions.domain: Automated program repair / synthetic data generation
contributions.source_quote: Second, we can leverage the diffusion model to generate an arbitrary amount of training data for other last-mile repair approaches (that are computationally more efficient) by sampling an intermediate program (input) and the final program (output) from the diffusion process.

self_declared_provenance.quote: In previous work, mistakes are introduced in the discrete token space, by implementing specialized functions that imitate human errors (Yasunaga & Liang, 2020; Joshi et al., 2024) and optionally training a neural network to imitate those (Yasunaga & Liang, 2021). Our aim is to show that the space of discrete representations encountered during the reverse diffusion process shares enough similarities to the discrete errors that humans make

In the following three sections, we respectively reiterate the components and training process of CODEFUSION (Singh et al., 2023a), describe how to apply it to problem of last-mile repair (building directly on the pre-trained CodeFusion model)

For Python, we use the popular BIFI (Yasunaga & Liang, 2021) model ... For Excel, we use the 17 operators used to fine-tune FLAME (Joshi et al., 2024) on last-mile formula repair. (baselines the synthetic data generator against these)

notes: Rejected. Contains honest trade-off/negative findings: the direct-repair application underperforms strong dedicated systems (BIFI, LaMirage) and GPT-4o/RING with compiler feedback - authors concede 'these very powerful models ... still perform better.' Repair success is noise-level dependent with a decline at high noise (too many changes); optimal injection point differs by language (Excel later, Python/PowerShell earlier). Authors position the synthetic-data-generation use case as the more promising of the two, implying the direct-repair use case is weaker.
